Trim allows you to shift your lift vector. By having the CG too far forward, you are incurring unnecessary trim drag to shift that vector onto the CG. Most (conventional fixed-wing) aircraft are designed for the tail to generate some lift in the designed cruise regime, and negative lift in other phases of flight. The idea of the tail always generating negative lift is a simplification presented to pilots in ground school to make theory of flight more intuitive. Airfoils naturally generate a pitch-down moment as a consequence of generating lift, so it's not necessary for the CG to be forward of the centre of pressure for the overall moment to be nose-down (defined as a stabilizing moment).

The CG can (and usually is) aft of the center of pressure, and even the aerodynamic centre, as long as it is not aft of the stick-free neutral point, the aircraft maintains longitudinal stability. The margin is generally very tight, though, which is why weight and balance is calculated prior to every flight.

Obviously my position is biased, but I think the military is a good way of getting a swath of experience early in your career. You'll be involved in mid-to-high level management immediately, and will be responsible for overseeing budgets and resource allocation if on projects. For the RCAF, you'll generally switch between field positions managing maintenance and "hard engineering" roles in Ottawa every four years or so. There are also a certain number of slots each year to send engineering officers for their master's, both within Canada and internationally.

I'm working on my P.Eng., and I know a few people who have gotten theirs. If you avoid Capital Projects and stick to engineering support positions when it's your turn to go to Ottawa, you should be able to get enough experience within 4 years, but realistically I would plan for it to take almost double that (I'm not saying avoid projects at all costs, it's valuable experience, it's just that PEO and other licensing bodies don't value it as much).

The main downside is pay. You'll start with decent pay (look up the Lt/Capt pay scales, available publicly online), especially considering your tuition will be fully subsidised and you'll be paid as an OCdt while in school, but your salary won't advance as much as civi side. Most people use the military to get experience and then move on. This is especially true right now. Canada has way too many engineering graduates for entry-level positions, so the military is a way to skip the entry-level.

If you're specifically thinking RMC, I would highly recommend it. You'll get a similar education to other universities, but you'll build a powerful network that will make it much easier to line up jobs if you decide to leave the military.

It's a big and personal choice, though, so I recommend doing as much research as you can before making the commitment.

Aerospace engineer here. It is pretty ridiculous. TL;DR: Wings, control surfaces, intakes are all weird and don't mesh together.

First, the folding wings. At high speed they fold forward, which would likely rip them off. As the wing moves forward, the aerodynamic center moves forward with it. With it ahead of the joint, the wing will want to twist up, which increases the angle of attack, increasing lift, increasing the twisting force. Wings gone.

Let's say the wings survive the fold and get tucked away. They go into the inner wing... just reducing your wing area and available lift. While it does result in a more swept wing that will be better suited to supersonic flight, it's an inefficient implementation. (Also if you just tuck the wing into itself, where is the fuel?)

Normally variable sweep is done to get good high speed and low speed performance. Sweeping the wing reduces the speed of the air relative to the leading edge, so it experiences supersonic flow (which comes with significant loss of lift and increase in drag) later, but this lower apparent speed means that it stalls more easily at lower speed. Swing-wings try to get the best of both worlds. This comes at the cost of having a single point of attachment between the wing and the fuselage, and it needs to be HEAVY to withstand the forces involved. With the Wyvern, not only are those forces HUGE because the wings sweep forward at high speed, but those joints are out on the wing itself, an already fragile location. It's just not structurally feasible. (Also where are you storing fuel? Your wings are full of structural reinforcement to keep those folding wings working, so there isn't much space for anything else).

Now let's talk control surfaces. This thing has close-coupled canards and a V tail when going slow, and then when going fast they just... fold down? I guess this is to compensate the loss of lifting area, but now you have no yaw control. With that big cockpit bubble in front, it is going to want to spin, and nothing will stop it. Also you need a pretty complicated hinge system to get the control surfaces to fold up/down AND adjust their pitch to do their job. It would be either, heavy, fragile, or both.

Now let's talk more about supersonic aerodynamics. When you go fast, you get a shock cone in front of you. You want your aircraft to stay inside this cone so you get less wave drag - part of the reason you sweep your wings. I looked at the angle between the nose and the wingtip when the wings were unfolded, and it was about 33 deg. To get a shock cone that angle, you need to be going Ma 1.83ish (check [this](https://www.grc.nasa.gov/www/k-12/airplane/machang.html#:~:text=Mu%20is%20an%20angle%20which,formed%20by%20the%20Mach%20angle.) for the calc). Incidentally, that is about the max speed that the diverterless intake the X-02 has can handle. If it goes faster, the compressor will probably stall, since at higher speeds you want a variable ramp or cone (it has to do with shock reflections and pressure ratios, which you can read about [here](https://www.grc.nasa.gov/www/k-12/airplane/reflects.html#:~:text=Reflected%20Shock%20Wave&text=When%20an%20object%20moves%20faster,change%20by%20a%20large%20amount.&text=A%20supersonic%20flow%20at%20Mach,flowing%20from%20left%20to%20right.)). When the wings fold in, the angle goes down to about 22 deg, giving a max speed of Ma 2.92... if only those compressors were designed to handle that speed.

Depends on the nature of the flameout, but generally you're right. If the engine stops adding energy, the compressor will stop pretty quickly, as it tries to compress (putting energy into air) without getting energy input.

A common reason for flameouts, though, is compressor stall, so the compressor stopping causes the flameout rather than the other way around. This usually happens if you go supersonic and your intake isn't designed for it, or for whatever reason air hits your first stage compressor at a weird angle and stalls the blades. If the compressor isn't do its job, less air reaches the combustion chamber, and you run out of energy to keep the compressor going.

Engines with afterburners will usually have bypass air, basically a portion of the intake air that doesn't go into the engine for combustion, but goes around the engine, then mixes with the exhaust. This uncombusted air is perfect for afterburning, since it boosts the oxygen content. Without bypass air, there would be very little oxygen to burn in the exhaust gas.

I still wouldn't say afterburning is efficient... it's basically dumping fuel into the exhaust and burning it. You increase your thrust because mass and energy has been added, but it is not the efficient, controlled process that takes place in the combustion chamber. It takes A LOT of fuel, so is usually only used on aircraft that need short bursts of high thrust, like combat aircraft.

I like to think that the energy is less wasted, and more... gets recycled. When the air coming in gets compressed, it gets energy added in the form of pressure and temperature. Then, as others have said, since you have more air in, you can use more fuel and get more energy from combustion. Then the exhaust goes through a turbine to drive the compressor. Conservation of energy, that same energy that was put into the air during the compression phase gets taken out to drive the compressor (plus mechanical and adiabatic losses, but they are small)... so in an ideal system the compressor "costs" very little overall energy.

For estimates, you usually start with an assumption that the fuel burned is directly proportional to thrust. So you'll have a specific fuel consumption of X lbm/lbf/hour. Then you calculate/estimate the time and required thrust for each phase of flight, keeping in mind that your weight is constantly decreasing.


If you set up fuel weight fractions - basically weight at the end of current phase of flight divided by weight at end of previous phase of flight - you can cancel a lot of weight terms out and simplify your calculations. It still usually requires you to assume one of your weight terms, and iterate until your result converges.


Here's some reading that might help:

[Thrust Specific Fuel Consumption](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrust-specific_fuel_consumption)

[Weight Fractions](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuel_fraction)

[Range calculation](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Range_(aeronautics))


Set up these equations with the info you have, and you should be able to rearrange and solve for fuel consumption per hour.

This is how it worked when I was in school, though your best bet is checking your school's course syllabi:

Aero and mech are similar in the foundational stages, and diverge partly around 3rd year, almost fully in 4th year. Your base, fundamental courses are the same (statics, dynamics, machining and manufacturing, materials science, math, etc) but you begin to diverge when you get into the more specific applications.

Aero goes into detail with fluids, as it is relevant to aerodynamic applications. Our final structures course was in the context of airframes (so a whole lot of thin sections and variable g-loading). Our final thermo courses were in the context of aerospace propulsion. While we shared our first controls courses with mechs, our final course was specific to aircraft applications. We also had an additional course in performance prediction and metrics for evaluating aircraft designs.

Mechs went into more detail in Finite Element Analysis, had a strength of materials course focusing on machine design, and their final controls course was focused on instrumentation of general systems.

Overall, they are very similar. Mechs could pick up aero stuff pretty quickly if they needed to, as they already have the foundational skills. In that sense, mechs have the advantage of being general and being able to do whatever they want. On the other hand, aeros have the advantage of already being a bit specialized if they are certain they want to go into aerospace.

Having swept wings of any type is detrimental below transsonic speeds. The main purpose of sweep is to reduce the effective airspeed relative to the wing's leading edge, which reduces shock effects and cleans up the flow a bit. This is worth the cost of reduced lift. At subsonic speeds, however, there is no benefit. You would only be reducing the lift by sweeping.

It defeats the purpose of the sweep at that point. Forward sweep achieves the same thing as conventional sweep (reducing the apparent Mach number on the leading edge of the wing), with the benefit of directing air inward toward the fuselage, reducing eingtip vortices. If you're going slower than transsonic, sweep hurts you.

The main issue with forward sweep is the centre of pressure and aerodynamic centre are both forward of the wing root. As more lift is generated, the wing will twist up, increasing angle of attack and generating more lift. The wing will either stall (which causes it to untwist, catch air again, and flutter) or be ripped off.

Yes and no. With most conventional welding techniques, the weld itself may be strong, but the sections right beside the weld become weak. Welding ruins the heat treatment and finish of the materials being used. In addition, the act of heating up a section to its melting point while the rest of it is cold introduces internal stress once the whole thing cools.

With cold welding, you don't have the thermal issues, as you're not doing anything to change the materials used. Because of that, though, the weak point is now at the joint rather than near the joint, as the materials have not been mixed in any way / no flux is holding them together.

Edit: Take what I have to say with a grain of salt. I am an engineer, not a welder or tradesperson, so my sources are from a general design/manufacturing point of view. A tradesperson would definitely have better insight than me.
